rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3; two-season field experiment (2009, 2010) in a commercial drip-irrigated olive orchard in La Rioja, Argentina, with four irrigation levels (100, 66, 33, 0% ETc) in a randomized complete block design, measuring soil water, stem water potential, leaf conductance, sap flow and trunk diameter variations.
rows.notes: The study uses drip irrigation as the delivery system for all treatments but reports no result of its own on drip as an application method controlling soil evaporation or deep percolation. It does not compare drip with any other method and does not measure evaporation or percolation; soil evaporation values mentioned in the Introduction are cited from earlier work (Figuerola et al., 2013; Rousseaux et al., 2009). What it actually shows is the response of soil REW and plant indicators to post-harvest regulated deficit irrigation and their relationships for scheduling purposes.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3; own two-season field experiment with RDI treatments, soil cores, pressure chamber, porometer, heat-balance sap flow sensors and continuous microdendrometers (Figs. 2-7, Tables 1-2).
rows.notes: The study evaluates the responsiveness and signal-to-noise of soil and plant indicators (including continuously recorded trunk diameter) to deficit irrigation and derives relationships/thresholds that could be used for scheduling. It does not implement sensor-, automation- or controller-driven dynamic scheduling, nor does it measure any water saving from such scheduling; irrigation was applied as fixed percentages of FAO56 ETc. The suggestion that automated soil moisture sensors or dendrometers could schedule irrigation is a recommendation/potential, i.e. a precondition of the claimed effect, not a demonstration of it.

notes: Full text appears complete. Primary field study on post-harvest RDI in olive; the cited claims about drip controlling evaporation/percolation and about sensor-driven dynamic scheduling are not results reported by this study.
